mcqs.q: Why does supraperiosteal (infiltration) anaesthesia work reliably in the maxilla?
opts: The maxilla has a thin, porous cortex through which the solution diffuses to the apex
The maxillary bone is dense and impermeable
The maxilla has no nerve supply
The solution is injected directly into the pulp
mcqs.explain: The maxilla's thin, porous facial cortex lets LA deposited at the apex diffuse through to the terminal dental plexus fibres.

mcqs.q: The middle superior alveolar (MSA) nerve is present in approximately what percentage of people?
mcqs.explain: The MSA nerve is present in only about 28% of the population; when present it supplies the premolars and the MB root of the first molar.

mcqs.q: For an infiltration injection, the needle insertion point is the intersection of:
opts: A horizontal line at the mucobuccal fold and a vertical line along the tooth's long axis
The midline and the occlusal plane
The gingival margin and the incisive papilla
Two lines over the greater palatine foramen
mcqs.explain: Insertion is where a horizontal line parallel to the mucobuccal fold meets a vertical line parallel to the target tooth's long axis.

mcqs.q: During a labial infiltration, the needle bevel should be oriented:
opts: Toward the bone, with the syringe at about 45° to the buccal plate
mcqs.explain: The syringe is held in line with the tooth's long axis at ~45° to the buccal plate, with the bevel facing bone.

mcqs.q: Infiltration over a child's permanent maxillary first molar may fail because its apex can lie in:
mcqs.explain: Infiltration is a relative contraindication there because the first molar apex may be located in dense zygomatic bone, blocking diffusion.

mcqs.q: The PSA (tuberosity) block anaesthetises the maxillary molars, but commonly misses the:
opts: Mesiobuccal root of the first molar (in ~28%)
Distobuccal root of the third molar
Palatal root of the second molar
mcqs.explain: In about 28% of patients the mesiobuccal root of the first molar (supplied by the MSA) is not anaesthetised by a PSA block.

mcqs.q: The PSA block is contraindicated in a patient who is:
mcqs.explain: Because of the haematoma risk, the PSA block is avoided in patients with bleeding tendencies (haemophilia, anticoagulants).

mcqs.q: In a PSA block, the needle is advanced from the mucobuccal fold above the 2nd molar in an:
opts: Upward, inward and posterior direction to about 16 mm
Downward and forward direction to 30 mm
mcqs.explain: A short (20 mm) needle is advanced upward, inward and posterior to ~16 mm, then after negative aspiration 1–1.5 mL is deposited.

mcqs.q: Over-insertion in a PSA block can cause a haematoma by penetrating the:
opts: Pterygoid venous plexus and maxillary artery
mcqs.explain: If advanced too far distally, the needle may pierce the pterygoid plexus and maxillary artery, causing a haematoma in the infratemporal fossa (bluish-red facial swelling).

mcqs.q: The MSA nerve block is specifically indicated when:
opts: An ASA block fails to anaesthetise teeth distal to the canine
Only the central incisors need anaesthesia
A mandibular molar is being treated
mcqs.explain: When the ASA block fails to anaesthetise the premolars (distal to the canine), the MSA block is used for the premolars and MB root of the first molar.

mcqs.q: An infraorbital (ASA) nerve block anaesthetises which nerves as the solution diffuses up the canal?
opts: The anterior AND middle superior alveolar nerves
Only the posterior superior alveolar nerve
The greater and lesser palatine nerves
mcqs.explain: LA at the infraorbital foramen diffuses up the canal to block the ASA and MSA nerves (plus infraorbital cutaneous branches).

mcqs.q: The infraorbital foramen is located by sliding a finger down from the infraorbital notch until you feel a:
mcqs.explain: Below the notch the bone is convex; continuing inferiorly a concavity (the foramen) is felt, and pressing the nerve against bone gives mild soreness.

mcqs.q: Besides the anterior teeth, an infraorbital block also numbs the:
opts: Lower eyelid, side of the nose and upper lip
Tongue and floor of the mouth
mcqs.explain: Its infraorbital cutaneous branches (inferior palpebral, lateral nasal, superior labial) anaesthetise the lower eyelid, side of nose and upper lip.

mcqs.q: Why is firm finger pressure maintained over the infraorbital foramen during the ASA block?
opts: To drive the solution into the foramen and up the canal
mcqs.explain: Maintaining pressure increases diffusion of the LA into the infraorbital foramen and canal, improving the block.

mcqs.q: Palatal injections are painful mainly because the palatal soft tissue is:
opts: Dense and firmly adherent to bone
mcqs.explain: The dense palatal mucosa is firmly bound to bone, so injection (especially rapid) raises tissue pressure and causes pain — hence slow injection is advised.

mcqs.q: Pressure anaesthesia (e.g. with a cotton applicator) reduces palatal injection pain by:
opts: Producing ischaemia so needle insertion is painless
mcqs.explain: Firm pressure with a blunt object produces ischaemia at the site, making needle insertion painless.

mcqs.q: For local infiltration of the palate, the needle is inserted from the gingival margin by about:
mcqs.explain: Insert 5–10 mm from the gingival margin and deposit only 0.2–0.3 mL; large volumes cause sloughing and ulceration of the palatal mucosa.

mcqs.q: The greater palatine foramen is located:
opts: Distal to the maxillary second molar, on the palatal side
Behind the central incisors at the midline
In the floor of the nose
mcqs.explain: The greater palatine foramen lies distal to the maxillary second molar on the palatal side; the block covers the palatal molars and premolars.

mcqs.q: In a greater palatine block, once the needle reaches bone the volume deposited is about:
mcqs.explain: After advancing ~5 mm into ischaemic tissue to bone, 0.45–0.6 mL is injected slowly.

mcqs.q: The nasopalatine block targets palatal tissue:
opts: Lateral to the incisive papilla (not into the papilla)
mcqs.explain: Because the incisive papilla is very sensitive, the injection is made lateral to it and advanced toward the incisive foramen.

mcqs.q: In a nasopalatine block, the needle should NOT be advanced more than 5 mm because it may:
opts: Enter the floor of the nose and cause infection
mcqs.explain: Advancing >5 mm into the incisive canal risks entering the floor of the nose, which can cause infection.

mcqs.q: Inadequate anaesthesia of the maxillary canine after a nasopalatine block is usually due to:
opts: Overlapping fibres from the greater palatine nerve
mcqs.explain: Overlapping greater palatine fibres can leave the canine region under-anaesthetised after a nasopalatine block.

mcqs.q: A PSA block is particularly indicated when:
opts: Two or more maxillary molars are to be extracted
Only a single incisor needs treatment
A lower molar is being restored
mcqs.explain: The PSA block is indicated when supraperiosteal injection is contraindicated or when two or more molar extractions are planned.

mcqs.q: Which objective sign confirms successful pulpal anaesthesia after an infiltration?
opts: No response to maximal electric pulp testing (80/80)
mcqs.explain: Objective confirmation is no response to maximal EPT output (80/80), alongside subjective numbness and painless treatment.

mcqs.q: A common cause of failed maxillary infiltration is the needle tip being:
opts: Below the apex or away from the bone
Exactly at the apex against bone
mcqs.explain: Failures occur when the needle tip is below the tooth apex or held away from the bone, so the solution doesn't reach the apical plexus.

saqs.q: State the nerve supply of the maxillary teeth and why infiltration succeeds there.
saqs.a: ASA — incisors/canine; MSA (in ~28%) — premolars + MB root of 1st molar; PSA — molars. Infiltration works because the maxilla has a thin, porous cortex through which LA diffuses to the apex.

saqs.q: Describe the landmarks and technique of maxillary infiltration.
saqs.a: Insert where a horizontal line at the mucobuccal fold meets a vertical line along the tooth's long axis; syringe at ~45° to the buccal plate, bevel toward bone, depositing at the apex.

saqs.q: Give the technique and main complication of the PSA block.
saqs.a: Short (20 mm) needle at the mucobuccal fold above the 2nd molar, advanced up/in/back ~16 mm; aspirate, inject 1–1.5 mL. Main complication: haematoma (pterygoid plexus/maxillary artery) if over-inserted.

saqs.q: Which nerves and teeth does the infraorbital (ASA) block cover, and how is the foramen located?
saqs.a: Blocks the ASA + MSA → incisors to premolars (+ MB root of 1st molar) and lower eyelid/nose/upper lip. Locate by feeling the infraorbital notch then sliding down to the concave foramen; keep pressure on it during injection.

saqs.q: List the steps for atraumatic palatal anaesthesia.
saqs.a: Apply topical, use pressure anaesthesia (ischaemia), maintain needle control, and inject very slowly.
Anaesthetises the palatal gingiva/mucosa of molars & premolars. The foramen is distal to the 2nd molar; approach from the opposite side, advance ~5 mm to bone, inject 0.45–0.6 mL.

saqs.q: Describe the nasopalatine block and its precautions.
saqs.a: Blocks the nasopalatine nerves bilaterally for the anterior palate; inject lateral to the incisive papilla, advance ≤5 mm toward the incisive foramen, deposit 0.45 mL slowly. Don't enter the papilla; >5 mm may reach the floor of the nose (infection).
